title: Read to the dying
hook: the text is read aloud to the dying and the dead

segments.voice: Yesterday, peaceful and wrathful: calm figures and fierce ones, and one instruction for both. Your line was your own mind. When a strong mood came, did you ask whose mind was showing it? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

A small room, the lamps low. Someone has just died, or is very close to it. Beside the bed sits a monk, or a family friend who knows how, with a long, narrow book on their knees. The pages are loose, printed in Tibetan, held between two boards. And they are reading out loud. Not to the family, though the family hears it. Not to themselves. They are reading to the person who is dying, and they will keep reading to them after the breathing stops. That is what this book was made for.
screen: `A LOW-LIT ROOM.` → `A BOOK ON SOMEONE'S KNEES.` → `READ TO THE ONE WHO IS DYING.`

segments.voice: First, the name. The text we've been opening this week is called the Bardo Thodol, which means liberation through hearing in the in-between. Hearing. The whole name rests on it. It isn't mainly a book for scholars to study at a desk. It is a book to be spoken into someone's ear. Second, who it speaks to. The reader addresses the one who has died by name and talks to them directly, the way a guide talks to a traveler on a dark road: this is the clear light, recognize it. These visions are your own mind; don't be afraid. Tradition holds that awareness goes on hearing after the body has gone quiet, and so the reading goes on too, through the days of the in-between. Third, where it came from. Tibetan tradition says Padmasambhava taught it and hid it as a treasure, and that a treasure-revealer, Karma Lingpa, brought it to light long afterward. Fourth, who it's for besides the dead. Some teachers say the book is meant to be heard long before the end: read in life, so the words are already familiar when they are needed most. And it shapes the living in the room. Someone sitting by a deathbed, with nothing to fix, is given something to do with their voice. That's a look back across this week too: the great seal and the great perfection, the teacher face to face, the in-between, the clear light, the two walls of visions. All of it, in the end, carried by a human voice reading aloud.
screen: `LIBERATION THROUGH HEARING.` · `SPOKEN TO THE ONE WHO DIED.` · `A HIDDEN TREASURE, TRADITION SAYS.` · `READ IN LIFE, HEARD AT THE END.` · then, large: `READ ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Find something kind to read: a verse from the Dhammapada, a few lines from a book you love, a letter someone once wrote you. Settle for a breath or two. Then read it aloud, slowly, at a speaking volume, as if someone you care about were sitting beside you and needed to hear it. Let the words land before you go on. When you've finished, sit quietly and let the sound fade. If you have someone in mind, let it be for them. The bell holds the time.
Read to the dying. The Tibetan practice of speaking the Bardo Thodol aloud to the one who is dying, and to the one who has died. Today's word.
Your line: read aloud. Today, read one kind thing out loud to someone: a child, a friend, an old relative on the phone. That closes the week. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: In Tibetan communities, a lama, monk or trained friend may read the Bardo Thodol aloud beside someone who is dying and continue reading after death, speaking directly to the one who has died through the days of the in-between.

original.note: Tibetan bar do thos grol: the in-between, hearing, liberation. Liberation through hearing in the in-between.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spooky book about the afterlife.
what it means: a guide read aloud to the dying and the dead, telling them to recognize what they meet.
what a scholar hears: bar do thos grol, liberation through hearing; a treasure text tradition credits to Padmasambhava and Karma Lingpa.
